question: What activities, in what order, make up the life of a data warehouse project from planning to maintenance, and which practices and mistakes matter at each step?
contributions: Readiness, scoping, justification and staffing guidance
Eight-step technical architecture process and product selection tasks
Physical design (aggregation, indexing, partitioning) and dimension/fact staging steps
Deployment, maintenance, growth and ten common mistakes

limits: No experiments or data: recommendations rest on the authors' project experience.
Era-bound: references CD-ROM, OLAP cubes, bit-mapped and B-tree indexes, FTP, aggregate navigators; no cloud warehouses, ELT, CDC or streaming.
Staging coverage is ETL-centric and batch; it says 'many teams focus solely on the E and the L' but gives little on extraction mechanics.
Defers detailed treatment to The Data Warehouse Lifecycle Toolkit (Wiley, 1998).
practices: Select products only after the technical architecture exists; product selection is not the first box (p.332, p.351).
Start with a single business process and a single source; avoid a customer-profitability mart as the first deliverable (p.336, Mistake 2 p.368).
Build iteratively on a lightweight bus architecture of conformed dimensions and facts rather than a comprehensive upfront analysis (Mistake 5, p.368).
Stage dimensions before facts: publish all dimensions of a schema before staging fact data (p.359).
Keep a persistent master cross-reference table per dimension with surrogate key, operational key, effective/expiration dates, most-recent indicator and CRC (Fig 16.3, p.359).
Compare CRC to detect changed dimension rows; overwrite type 1/3 attributes, add a new row for type 2 and expire the prior row (p.360).
Maintain a two-column most-recent surrogate key assignment table for fast fact key lookups (p.360).
Separate fact data by grain early in staging (p.361).

Enforce referential integrity during staging, not at load; handle unmatched keys by halting, a reloadable suspense file, or a new per-key 'Description Unknown for Operational Key XYZ' dimension row rather than one shared dummy key (p.361-362).
On fact load key collisions: halt, write to suspense file, or additively update the target row (p.362).
Collect audit statistics at extract and compare row counts and cross-foots after transform (p.359, p.362).
Prefer a commercial staging tool for metadata integration, reusability and maintainability, accepting no first-iteration payback (p.358).
Normalizing source data in staging is often unnecessary; treat it as a comfort zone, not a requirement (p.358).
Build aggregates as their own physical fact tables with shrunken conformed dimensions, driven by usage patterns and data distribution, plus an aggregate navigator (p.356).

Index dimension tables with a unique PK index, B-tree on high-cardinality constrained attributes and bit-mapped on low/medium cardinality; fact tables get a concatenated index led by the date key plus single indexes on other foreign keys (p.357).
Partition large fact tables by date (month, quarter or year) so queries touch fewer partitions, loads rebuild only one partition's index and old partitions archive easily (p.357).
Turn on usage monitoring early (p.357).
Assess data feasibility early: there is no short-term fix if clean source data at the right grain is not being collected (p.335).
Interview business users about what they do and decide on, not grain; interleave data-centric interviews with source system experts (p.341, p.345).
Do not design to an agreed 'top five reports'; user questions will change (p.344).
Use surveys not at all for requirements; use interviews plus facilitated sessions (p.341).
Prioritize with an impact versus feasibility quadrant; do the high-impact, high-feasibility cell first (Fig 16.2, p.347).
Deliver parameter-driven analytic applications, since business users will not build their own (Mistake 6, p.367).
Release in alpha (project team), beta (limited users), then controlled general availability (p.365).
Treat the warehouse as production after deployment, with service level agreements and proactive monitoring of performance and capacity (p.366).
Freeze features at rollout and negotiate scope changes in the implementation stage; handle changes by adding resources, trading scope, or logging an enhancement request (p.340, Mistake 3 p.368).
Get source-system owners to partner with the warehouse team, and senior executives involved before launch (Mistakes 10 and 4, p.367-368).

terms.definition: the approach drawn from The Data Warehouse Lifecycle Toolkit: focus on business needs, present dimensional data, and give each implementation a finite cycle
quick and dirty demonstrations of the potential capabilities of a data warehouse; a sales tool rather than a technical proof of design
too firm of a commitment to too brief of a timeline involving too many source systems and too many users in too many locations with too diverse analytic requirements
positions staffed from either business or IT: technical resources that understand the business or business resources that understand technology
rows are business processes, columns are organizational groups or functions (not a bus matrix)
prioritization with business impact on the vertical axis and feasibility on the horizontal axis
functionality between the client and the RDBMS that intercepts SQL and rewrites it to use appropriate aggregates
the party responsible for defining, maintaining and publishing a particular dimension for the data marts; publishing is a kind of synchronous replication
persistent staging table tracking the surrogate key assigned to an operational key at a point in time, with attribute profile, dates, most-recent indicator and CRC

terms.term: Most recent surrogate key assignment table
terms.definition: two columns, operational source key and its most recent surrogate key, for fast lookups when assigning fact table surrogate keys
